vector_name: RFC 8785 Appendix B extended test data (numbers, string, literals, whitespace)
rule: RFC 8785 Appendix B (extended test data, expected output as published); mechanics: §3.2.2.2 string escaping (short forms \b\t\n\f\r, remaining C0 as lowercase 4-hex, no solidus escape), §3.2.2.3 numbers via ES6 §7.1.12.1 shortest round-trip, §3.2.3 key sorting, no insignificant whitespace.
divergence_trap: Python json.dumps(sort_keys=True) escapes € as \u20ac (ensure_ascii default); literal-preserving serializers keep '4.50' and '1E30' verbatim instead of '4.5'/'1e+30'. JS JSON.stringify with sorted keys happens to match (JCS was modeled on it), which falsely reassures non-JS porters.

vector_name: Negative zero and zero with fraction
rule: §3.2.2.3: numbers are IEEE-754 doubles serialized per ES6 Number::toString; ±0 maps to '0', and integral values print without a fractional part.
divergence_trap: serde_json emits '-0.0' for -0.0; Python json.dumps(-0.0) → '-0.0'; Go emits '-0'; Python also emits '0.0' for 0.0 — all preserve the sign/dot the canonical form must drop.

rule: §3.1/§3.2.2.3: all input numbers are converted to IEEE-754 double before canonicalization. 9007199254740993 (2^53+1, odd) is not representable and rounds ties-to-even to 9007199254740992; 9007199254740994 is exactly representable.
divergence_trap: Any parser that preserves arbitrary precision — Python json.loads (int), Java BigDecimal, lossless-json — re-emits 9007199254740993 and the 'canonical' bytes differ from the double-conforming form.

rule: §3.2.2.3 via ES6 §7.1.12.1: fixed notation for 1e-6 ≤ |x| < 1e21, exponential for |x| ≥ 1e21; exponential form is lowercase 'e', carries '+', and has no zero-padded exponent digits.
divergence_trap: Python repr and Go strconv emit '1e+20' for 1e20 (they switch to exponential far below ES6's 1e21 threshold); C printf-style emitters pad exponents ('1e+021') or omit the '+' ('1e21').

rule: §3.2.2.3 via ES6 §7.1.12.1: |x| ≥ 1e-6 uses fixed notation ('0.000001'); |x| < 1e-6 switches to exponential with unpadded negative exponent ('1e-7').
divergence_trap: Python repr(1e-6)='1e-06' and repr(1e-7)='1e-07' (zero-padded two-digit exponent, wrong threshold); decimal-only formatters emit '0.0000001' for 1e-7.

rule: §3.2.2.3 via ES6 §7.1.12.1: output is the shortest string that round-trips the double — no trailing '.0', and the input's literal exponent form is never preserved.
divergence_trap: serde_json and Python emit '1.0' for 1.0; literal-preserving canonicalizers keep '1e2' or emit '100.0'.

vector_name: Control characters, short escapes, lowercase hex, and unescaped DEL
rule:
§3.2.2.2: only U+0000–U+001F, '"' and '\' are escaped;   	 
    use short forms, remaining C0 use lowercase 4-hex \u00xx; U+007F (DEL) is outside the escaped set and is emitted verbatim.
divergence_trap: Libraries that escape DEL ('\u007F') or emit uppercase hex ('\u001F', '\u000F') diverge; the canonical output's DEL is a raw 0x7F byte, and any uppercase-hex or DEL-escaping implementation fails byte comparison.

vector_name: Solidus, non-ASCII, and surrogate pair emitted verbatim
rule: §3.2.2.2: '/' (solidus) is NOT escaped; non-ASCII characters — including astral-plane characters represented by surrogate pairs — are emitted verbatim as UTF-8, never as \uXXXX.
divergence_trap: PHP json_encode (default flags) and ASP.NET JavaScriptSerializer emit '\/' for '/' and '\u20ac'/'\ud83d\ude00' escapes for the non-ASCII characters.

vector_name: UTF-16 code-unit ordering vs code-point ordering (astral vs U+E000–U+FFFF)
rule: §3.2.3: object members are sorted lexicographically by UTF-16 code unit values. '😀' = D83D DE00, 'ﬀ' = FB00, ' ' = FFFD; 0xD83D < 0xFB00 < 0xFFFD, so the astral key sorts FIRST even though its code point (U+1F600) is the largest.
divergence_trap: Code-point sorting (equivalently UTF-8 byte comparison, e.g. Python sorted(), Rust BTreeMap<&str>) yields ﬀ,  , 😀 — the astral key moves from first position to last; this is the classic JCS-vs-UTF-8-sorter divergence.

vector_name: No Unicode normalization: canonically equivalent keys stay distinct (U+03A9 omega vs U+2126 ohm sign)
rule: §3.2.2.2: strings are serialized verbatim — JCS applies NO Unicode normalization (NFC(U+2126) = U+03A9, but JCS must not perform it); §3.2.3 orders by UTF-16 units: 0x03A9 < 0x2126. First key is U+03A9 (Greek capital omega), second is U+2126 (ohm sign).
divergence_trap: An implementation that NFC-normalizes before serializing (a habit from RDF/JSON-LD canonicalization) merges the two canonically equivalent keys into a single member, changing both the key set and the byte output.

vector_name: Empty containers, nested structures, and array order preservation
rule: §3.2.3 sorts only object member names ('empty_arr' < 'empty_obj' < 'nested'; 'arr' < 'x'); arrays are ordered values and their element order MUST NOT be sorted; structures serialize compactly with no whitespace; empty containers are preserved.
divergence_trap: Pretty-printers inject spaces/newlines; over-eager canonicalizers sort array contents ([3,1,2] → [1,2,3]) or drop empty containers — both produce wrong canonical bytes.

vector_name: Duplicate object keys are illegal input
canonical_output: ERROR: duplicate member name 'a' — input rejected; JCS defines no canonical form for duplicate keys
rule: §3.1 (JCS input requirements: valid JSON with unique member names; canonicalization presupposes a one-to-one mapping) and Appendix B, which treats duplicate object keys as out-of-scope/undefined rather than defining a winner.
divergence_trap: JS JSON.parse silently keeps the last value ({"a":2}) while several other parsers keep the first ({"a":1}) — both emit a plausible-looking 'canonical' document, so signatures over either form are malleable and canonicalization-based checks can be bypassed; a conforming implementation must reject instead.
